Keep the 1/2 cup softened butter at the mixing area rather than by the burner. You'll use it with the sugars after the chocolate is melted, so it should be soft enough to cream smoothly.
I have the butter softening on the counter. What sugars do I need to measure?
Measure 1/2 cup white sugar and 1/2 cup packed brown sugar. Pack the brown sugar firmly into the measuring cup, then keep both sugars with the softened butter for the creaming step.
The sugars are measured, and I'm turning to the stove with the chocolate chips.
Put the chocolate chips into the heavy saucepan over very low heat. Let them begin to melt slowly, and keep the pan from getting hot enough to scorch the chocolate.
The chips are glossy around the edges but still holding their shape in the middle.
Start stirring gently so the softened chocolate blends with the firmer chips. Keep stirring until the chocolate is evenly melted and smooth, still over very low heat.
It looks smooth now. Should I leave it on the burner while I mix the butter and sugars?
Once it's evenly melted, take it off the heat so it doesn't keep cooking. Then cream the softened butter with the white sugar and packed brown sugar until the mixture looks lighter and fluffier.
The butter and sugars are mixing, but there are a few brown sugar lumps.
Keep creaming a little longer and press any visible lumps against the side of the bowl with your spatula. You're aiming for a light texture before the eggs go in.
The mixture is lighter now, and I have the eggs nearby. How should I add them?

Beat in the eggs one at a time, mixing after each addition until it disappears into the butter-sugar mixture before adding the next. After that, check that the batter looks evenly blended before you continue with the rest of your recipe.
Can you talk me through Carrot Pineapple Cake I while I get set up? I'm using a 9x13 inch pan.

Absolutely. Put the 9x13 inch pan on your counter, then gather the dry ingredients you'll measure first: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 2 teaspoons baking soda, 1 teaspoon baking powder, and 1 teaspoon salt.
The flour, baking soda, baking powder, and salt are out. Should I heat the oven yet or prep the pan first?
Go ahead and preheat the oven to 350 degrees F, which is 175 degrees C. While it heats, grease and flour the 9x13 inch pan so the cake releases cleanly later.
Oven is heating, and I've greased the pan. How much flour goes into the bowl?
Measure 2 cups all-purpose flour into a mixing bowl. Add 2 teaspoons baking soda, 1 teaspoon baking powder, and 1 teaspoon salt with it.
Those are in the bowl. The recipe also mentions cinnamon in the dry mix, but I don't see an amount here.

Since the amount isn't shown in what you have, don't guess if you're trying to follow it closely. Just note that the dry step says to mix flour, baking soda, baking powder, salt, and cinnamon together.
I'll keep that in mind. Do I need to sift, or can I whisk the dry ingredients?
Whisking is fine here. Stir the flour, baking soda, baking powder, salt, and cinnamon until the leavening and salt are evenly dispersed, with no little pockets of powder.
The dry bowl looks even. What happens before the wet ingredients go in?
Make a well in the center of the dry mixture. That hollow gives you a spot to add the sugar, oil, eggs, and vanilla without scattering everything over the sides of the bowl.
The well is made. I have the sugar, oil, eggs, and vanilla ready, but no amounts are written in my note.

Add them only according to the amounts on your full recipe card if you have it nearby. From the steps we're using, the action is to add sugar, oil, eggs, and vanilla into the well, then bring the mixture together gently.
Once it's mixed, should I pour it straight into the prepared pan?

Yes. When the batter is combined, scrape it into the greased and floured 9x13 inch pan and spread it evenly. Keep the oven at 350 degrees F, or 175 degrees C, and check the cake's texture and doneness before serving.
I want to make Fresh Cranberry Spiced Tea today. Can you guide me through it while I get set up?
Absolutely. Put a large pot on the stove and have a strainer ready for later. You'll start with 1 pound of fresh or frozen cranberries and 3 quarts of cold water.
I've got the pot, cranberries, and water. Should I measure the juices now too, or wait?
Measure them now so the finishing part is easy: 2 cups orange juice and 2 1/8 cups pineapple juice. The recipe also calls for lemon juice and sugar to be stirred in at the end, so keep those nearby.
The cranberries are still frozen. Is that okay for the pot?
Yes, fresh or frozen cranberries both work here. Add the cranberries and the 3 quarts cold water to the large pot; the frozen berries may just take a little longer to come up to a boil.
They're in the water now. How high should I heat it?
Bring the pot to a boil over steady heat. Once it's boiling, cook only until the berries pop, which should be about 5 minutes.
Some berries are splitting already, but not all of them. What am I looking for?
You want the cranberries to pop and soften enough to release their color and flavor into the water. When most have burst and you're around that 5-minute mark, take the pot off the heat.
Okay, it smells tart and the liquid is red. Do I strain it right away?
Not yet. Remove it from the heat and let it stand at room temperature until cold; the recipe says this takes several hours.
Several hours is fine. Should I cover it while it cools on the counter?
You can loosely cover it once the steaming slows, but don't rush the cooling step. Letting it stand until cold is part of getting the cranberry flavor into the liquid.
It's cold now. I have the strainer over a bowl and the juices measured.

Strain out the cranberries, then stir the orange juice, pineapple juice, lemon juice, and sugar into the cranberry liquid. Once everything is dissolved and combined, taste it and chill or serve as you like.
I'm about to make Adriennes Tom Ka Gai. Can you help me get the prep organized before I turn on the stove?

Absolutely. Put a large saucepan on the stove but don't heat it yet. Measure out 2 teaspoons peanut oil, thinly slice 2 cloves garlic, grate 2 tablespoons fresh ginger root, and chop 1/4 cup lemon grass so those aromatics are ready to go in quickly.
Garlic, ginger, lemon grass, and oil are set. Should anything else be near the pan before I start cooking?

Yes. Keep the red pepper, coriander, and cumin within reach, since they cook with the aromatics. Also have the chicken and onion ready for the next addition, because once the spices smell fragrant you'll move on without much delay.
I have the large saucepan on medium heat now. Do I add the oil first?
Yes, heat the 2 teaspoons peanut oil in the large saucepan over medium heat. When the oil looks loose and shimmery, stir in the garlic, ginger, lemon grass, red pepper, coriander, and cumin.
The aromatics are in, and they smell strong pretty quickly. How long should I let them cook?
Cook them just until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Stir so the garlic and lemon grass don't sit in one hot spot; you're looking for a warm, spicy aroma rather than browning.
The mixture smells fragrant now. I have chicken and onion beside me—what should I watch for after adding them?
Stir in the chicken and onion, then keep everything moving as it cooks. The recipe cue is chicken turning white and onion becoming translucent, which should take about 5 minutes.
The chicken is mostly white and the onion looks soft and translucent. Is bok choy next?
Yes, stir in the bok choy. Let it cook until it begins to wilt, checking the texture as it softens; the timing range is 5 to 10 minutes.
The bok choy is starting to wilt but still has some body. Should I wait for it to collapse completely?
No need to cook it until it collapses. Once it has clearly begun to wilt and fits into the mixture more easily, you're ready for the liquid and finishing ingredients.
What should I add to finish the soup, and what final checks should I make before serving?

Stir in the water, coconut milk, fish sauce, and cilantro. Let everything come together, then check that the chicken is cooked through, the bok choy is tender-wilted, and the broth tastes balanced before serving Adriennes Tom Ka Gai.
Can you walk me through Anzac Biscuits I while I set up the counter and bake them?
Absolutely. Put out two mixing areas: one bowl for the dry ingredients and a small saucepan for the butter and syrup. You'll also want cookie sheets ready, greased or lined with baking paper.
I've got a bowl and saucepan out. Which dry ingredients should go in the bowl?
Add 1 cup quick cooking oats, 3/4 cup flaked coconut, 1 cup all-purpose flour, and 1 cup white sugar to the bowl. Stir them together so the oats, flour, sugar, and coconut are evenly mixed.
The dry bowl is mixed. I also have the baking soda nearby—does that go in yet?
Hold the baking soda for the wet mixture. Measure 1 teaspoon baking soda, but don't add it to the dry bowl. It gets mixed with boiling water before joining the melted butter and syrup.
Okay, the soda is measured. What should happen in the saucepan?
Put 1/2 cup butter and the syrup in the small saucepan over low heat. Warm them gently until the butter melts and the mixture is smooth; keep the heat low so it doesn't scorch.
The butter has melted into the syrup. I have boiling water ready.
Stir the 1 teaspoon baking soda into the boiling water, then add that foamy mixture to the melted butter and syrup. The saucepan mixture may bubble up, so pour and stir carefully.
It foamed a bit and looks combined. Do I pour it straight into the dry ingredients?
Yes. Pour the butter-syrup mixture into the oats, coconut, flour, and sugar, then stir until everything is evenly moistened. The dough should look cohesive enough to scoop, not like a loose batter.
The mixture is holding together. How should I shape them on the sheets?
Drop the mixture by teaspoons onto the greased cookie sheets or baking paper. Leave space between them because they can spread as they bake.
They're on the trays. What temperature and timing should I use?

Bake them at 350 degrees F, which is 175 degrees C, for 18 to 20 minutes. Check near the end for set edges and a lightly golden color, then let them settle briefly on the sheet before moving them to serve or cool.
I'm making Fudge Drops and want to get organized before the pan goes on. What should I set out?

Set out 1 2/3 cups sugar, 1 (5 ounce) can evaporated milk, 2 tablespoons butter or margarine, and 1/2 teaspoon salt. You'll also want a heavy saucepan, a stirring spoon, waxed paper, and baking sheets ready before you start heating.
I've got the sugar and evaporated milk measured. Should the baking sheets be prepared now or later?
Prepare them now. Line the baking sheets with waxed paper before the mixture cooks, because once the fudge mixture is ready you'll be dropping it by tablespoonfuls right away.
The sheets are lined, and the butter and salt are beside the stove. Do I add everything to the pan together?
Yes. Put the sugar, evaporated milk, butter or margarine, and salt into the heavy saucepan together. Give the pan a quick check so the bottom is heavy enough to help prevent scorching.
They're in the saucepan. The butter is still in one piece—should I wait for it to melt before stirring?
Start stirring as the pan heats over medium heat. The butter will melt into the sugar and milk while you stir, and the recipe wants constant stirring as the mixture comes to a boil.
It's warming and starting to look smoother. How do I know when I'm at the right point?
Keep the heat at medium and keep stirring until the mixture reaches a boil. Look for bubbling that continues across the mixture rather than just a few small bubbles at the edge.
It's boiling now, and I'm still stirring. Do I keep it on the burner?
Once it has reached the boil as directed, remove the saucepan from the heat. Then stir in the remaining ingredients called for on your recipe card.
The pan is off the heat and everything is stirred together. What should the setup look like for portioning?
Bring the waxed paper-lined baking sheets close to the pan. Use a tablespoon to scoop the mixture, then drop each spoonful onto the waxed paper with a little space between drops.
Some spoonfuls are landing a bit unevenly. Is that a problem for serving?
A little unevenness is fine for Fudge Drops. Focus on tablespoon-sized portions on the waxed paper-lined baking sheets, then let them sit until the texture is set enough to lift and serve.
I'm making apple butter spice cake. Can you help me get set up without overcomplicating it?
Absolutely. Heat the oven to 350 degrees F, or 175 degrees C, and grease or spray a 9x13 inch pan so it is ready before the batter comes together.
Pan is greased. What should I mix for the topping?
Stir together 1 cup packed brown sugar, 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon, 1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg, and 1/2 cup chopped pecans. Keep that bowl nearby; it gets layered with the batter later.
The topping smells good. Which dry ingredients should I handle next?
Sift the dry mixture together: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 teaspoon baking powder, baking soda, and salt. Sifting helps keep the cake crumb lighter and spreads the leavening evenly.
I have the dry bowl ready. How should I start the batter?
Blend the butter and sugar until they look smooth and a little lighter. Add the eggs and beat well before adding the apple butter, vanilla, and either wheat germ or bran cereal.
When I add the dry ingredients and sour cream, do I dump them all in?
Add the sifted dry ingredients alternately with the sour cream, mixing well after each addition. Stop once the batter looks even rather than continuing to beat it hard.
The batter is mixed. How do I build it in the pan with that pecan topping?
Pour 1/2 of the batter into the prepared pan, spread it gently, and sprinkle 1/2 of the topping over it. Add the remaining batter, then scatter the remaining topping across the surface.
It's layered and ready for the oven. How long should I bake it?
Bake it at 350 degrees F for about 40 minutes. Start checking near the end: the center should be set, and a tester should come out clean or with just a few moist crumbs.
If the top looks done before the middle, what should I watch for?

Look at the center more than the edges. The topping may darken because of the brown sugar and pecans, but the cake should not jiggle in the middle. Let it cool in the pan a bit before slicing so the layers hold together.
I'm making Cranberry Brandy Slush for tomorrow. I've got counter space cleared—what should I pull out before I start mixing?

Set out a large freezer-safe plastic container, a spoon or whisk, and the drink ingredients: 2 cups cherry brandy liqueur, one 16 ounce can frozen orange juice concentrate, one 16 ounce can frozen lemonade concentrate, and 2 quarts cranberry juice.
The orange juice and lemonade concentrates are still frozen solid. Do I need to thaw them first?
Let them soften enough that you can scrape or spoon them into the container and stir them smoothly. They don't need to be warm—just workable so they blend with the brandy and cranberry juice.
I have the plastic container ready. Should the brandy go in before the juices?

You can add them in any order, but it's easy to start with the cherry brandy liqueur and the two concentrates, then pour in the cranberry juice while stirring to loosen everything into one even mixture.
The mixture is mostly combined, but I see a few streaks of concentrate around the sides.
Scrape the sides and bottom of the container, then stir until the orange and lemonade concentrates are fully dispersed. You're looking for a uniform cranberry-colored liquid with no thick pockets.
It's mixed now. How much room should I leave in the container before freezing?
Leave a little headspace so the slush has room as it freezes, and make sure the lid is secure. Put the container in the freezer overnight.
Overnight is the full timing, right? I'm trying to plan when to serve it.
Yes, freeze it overnight so it becomes scoopable and icy. If you're serving tomorrow, keep it frozen until close to serving time, then scoop directly from the container.
When I take it out, what texture should I expect before adding soda?
It should be a firm frozen slush, not a pourable drink. Use a sturdy spoon or scoop to portion the desired amount into each glass.
I have lemon-lime soda chilling. How do I finish each glass without watering it down too much?
Scoop the frozen cranberry brandy mixture into the glass first, then fill the glass with chilled lemon-lime soda. Add the soda right before serving so the drink stays fizzy and slushy.
Can you walk me through Eggplant Mixed Grill? I've got the vegetables on the counter and want to keep it straightforward.
Absolutely. Start by getting a large resealable plastic bag ready for the marinade, since the vegetables will go into that before grilling.
What should I measure for the herb-and-oil part before I open the bag?
Measure 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley, 2 tablespoons chopped fresh oregano, and 2 tablespoons chopped fresh basil.
The herbs are chopped. What else goes into the bag with the olive oil?
Add the vinegar, kosher salt, pepper, and garlic to the bag with the olive oil, parsley, oregano, and basil, then mix everything together inside the bag.
I've got onion, asparagus, mushrooms, eggplant, and both peppers sliced. Do they all go in at once?
Yes. Put the onion, asparagus, mushrooms, eggplant, red bell pepper, and yellow bell pepper into the bag with the marinade.
The bag is pretty full. Should I shake it hard or handle it more gently?
Seal it well and turn the bag gently so the marinade coats the vegetables without bruising them or forcing liquid toward the seal.
How long does it need to sit, and where should I put it?
Marinate it for 2 hours in the refrigerator, turning the bag occasionally so the vegetables stay evenly coated.
The 2 hours are almost up. When should the grill come into play?
As the marinating time ends, preheat the grill for high heat so it is ready when the vegetables come out of the refrigerator.
Before I put the vegetables on, is there anything I should do to the grate?
Lightly oil the grill grate, then arrange the marinated vegetables on it for the mixed grill.
Can you walk me through Fried Chicken Tenders while I set up the counter?

Absolutely. Set up a simple breading station with three shallow bowls if you have them, plus a small bowl for the egg wash. You'll want the chicken nearby, with space to set the coated pieces aside before frying.
What should go into the dry bowls?

Put 1 cup all-purpose flour in one shallow bowl. In a separate shallow bowl, add 2 cups Italian-style seasoned bread crumbs, then mix in 1/2 teaspoon ground black pepper and 1/2 teaspoon cayenne pepper.
I've got those ready. What do I do with the eggs and water?
Beat 2 eggs with 2 tablespoons water in a small bowl. Keep that bowl between the flour and the breadcrumb mixture so each tender can move cleanly from dry to wet to crumb coating.
So the order is flour, egg, then crumbs, right?
Yes. Take one piece of chicken at a time, coat it in the flour, dip it into the eggs and water, then press it into the seasoned bread crumbs. Set each coated piece aside as you finish it.
How coated should they look before I start frying?

They should have an even breadcrumb layer with no large wet patches showing. If crumbs aren't sticking somewhere, lightly press that spot back into the breadcrumb bowl rather than piling on loose crumbs.
I'm ready to heat the oil. What temperature am I aiming for?
Heat the oil in a deep fryer to 375 degrees F, which is 190 degrees C. Let it come fully to temperature before adding chicken so the coating fries instead of soaking up oil.
Should I put all the tenders in at once if they fit?
Fry them in small batches. Give the pieces enough room so they don't crowd each other; that helps the breading stay crisp and the color develop evenly.
How long should each batch cook, and what should I check before serving?
Fry each small batch for 6 to 8 minutes, or until the tenders are golden brown. Before serving, check that the coating is crisp, the color is even, and the chicken is cooked through.
I'm making Basil Burgers on the outdoor grill. Can you walk me through setup through serving?
Absolutely. Start by preheating the outdoor grill to high heat so it's ready when the patties are formed. While it heats, clear space for a mixing bowl, a patty plate, and your ingredients.
I've got the bowl out. Which ingredients should I measure before touching the beef?
Measure 3 tablespoons Worcestershire sauce, 1 1/2 tablespoons dried basil, or more to taste, and 1/4 teaspoon garlic salt. Also keep pepper nearby for the mixture.
The grill is heating. I have 1 1/4 pounds ground beef in the bowl—do I add everything at once?
Yes. Add the Worcestershire sauce, dried basil, garlic salt, and pepper to the ground beef. Mix just until the seasonings look evenly distributed so the burgers don't get overworked.
The mixture smells good, but it's a little loose. Should I keep mixing it?
Stop once it holds together enough to shape. Divide the mixture into 4 portions and form burger patties, pressing them together gently rather than kneading them.
Patties are shaped. Anything I should do before they go onto the grill grate?
Lightly oil the grill grate before adding the patties. That helps with sticking, especially since you'll be turning them only once.
They're on the grill now. What timing am I aiming for?

Cook the burgers about 6 minutes total, turning once. Use an instant-read thermometer if you can, and aim for an internal temperature of 160 degrees F, which is 70 degrees C, unless you're cooking to another preferred doneness safely.
I'm ready to flip, but one patty is sticking a bit. Do I force it?
Give it a few more moments if it resists; a burger usually releases more cleanly once it has seared. Slide the spatula fully underneath, then turn it once and let the second side cook.
The thermometer is close to 160, and I'm getting ready to plate. What's the final check?
Check the thickest patty for 160 degrees F or 70 degrees C, make sure the surface looks browned, and let the burgers sit briefly before serving so the texture settles.
I'm making Gelatin Fruit Salad. I've got a saucepan, a mixing spoon, and a dish for chilling—can you walk me through it?

Absolutely. Set out 1 cup applesauce, 2 (3 ounce) packages cherry gelatin, 1 (12 ounce) can lemon-lime soda, and 1 (8 ounce) can crushed pineapple, undrained. You'll also want space in the refrigerator for the dish before you start heating.
The applesauce is measured, and the gelatin packets are open. Should the soda and pineapple be ready now too?
Yes, keep them close. Leave the crushed pineapple undrained, since the liquid goes into the salad, and open the lemon-lime soda so you can add it slowly once the gelatin is dissolved.
The saucepan is on the stove with the applesauce in it. How hot should I take it?
Heat the applesauce until it comes to a boil, stirring now and then so it doesn't scorch on the bottom. Once it reaches a boil, you won't keep cooking it there.
It just started bubbling around the edges and then across the middle.
Take the saucepan off the heat now. Stir in both 3 ounce packages of cherry gelatin until the granules are fully dissolved and the mixture looks smooth.
The gelatin has disappeared into the applesauce, and it looks glossy. Is it time for the soda?
Yes. Pour in the 12 ounce can of lemon-lime soda slowly, stirring gently as you add it so the fizz doesn't surge over the pan.
The soda is mixed in without overflowing. I still have the 8 ounce can of crushed pineapple with its juice.
Add the crushed pineapple undrained, including all the juice from the can. Stir just enough to distribute the fruit evenly through the gelatin mixture.
It's all mixed. Should I let it cool on the counter before putting it in the dish?
You can transfer it carefully to the serving dish or mold now, then refrigerate it. Make sure the dish is steady and not filled so high that it spills on the way to the fridge.
It's in the refrigerator. What am I looking for before serving?
Let it chill until firm. Before serving, check that it holds its shape when gently nudged or spooned, with the pineapple suspended throughout rather than the mixture still sloshing.
Can you walk me through the stovetop part of Alaskan Halibut Lasagna? I've got the skillet out and want to stay organized.

Absolutely. Set up the ingredients before turning on the heat: 6 tablespoons butter or margarine, divided; 1 1/2 pounds halibut steaks with the bones removed, cut into 1 inch cubes; 2 minced garlic cloves; and 3/4 teaspoon dried thyme.
The halibut is cubed and I checked for bones. How much butter goes into the pan at the start?
Put a large skillet over medium heat and melt 2 tablespoons of the butter. Keep the remaining butter aside since the recipe says the 6 tablespoons are divided.
The butter is melting but not browned. Should I wait for it to foam, or add the fish now?
Once the 2 tablespoons butter are fully melted and coating the skillet, you can add the halibut cubes. You don't need to brown the butter for this step.
Fish is in the skillet. Do the garlic and thyme go in right away with it?
Yes. Add the 2 minced garlic cloves and the 3/4 teaspoon dried thyme with the halibut, then gently spread everything so the fish cooks evenly.
I'm trying not to break up the cubes. What's the best way to stir this?
Use a wide spatula and turn the pieces gently rather than stirring hard. Keep the heat at medium so the garlic cooks with the fish without scorching.
How long should I expect the halibut to take from here?
Cook it until the fish flakes easily with a fork, about 10 minutes. Use that flaking texture as your main doneness check.
It's been close to 10 minutes. Some pieces flake, but the thickest cubes still look a little translucent in the center.
Give the thicker pieces another brief turn in the skillet and check again with a fork. They should flake easily and look opaque before you take them off the heat.
Okay, the halibut is opaque and flakes cleanly now. What should I do before it sits too long in the pan?
Remove the halibut mixture from the skillet and set it aside. Keep it in a bowl or plate ready for the next lasagna step, and don't leave it over the heat once it's done.
Can you walk me through making churros? I've got the saucepan out and want to set up before I turn on the heat.

Absolutely. Put a small saucepan on the stove, and set out 1 cup water, 2 1/2 tablespoons white sugar, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 2 tablespoons vegetable oil. Keep the flour nearby too, since it gets stirred in once the hot mixture comes off the heat.
I've measured the water, sugar, salt, and oil. Should I combine them cold in the pan or wait until it's warm?
Combine them in the small saucepan before heating: water, 2 1/2 tablespoons sugar, the salt, and 2 tablespoons vegetable oil all go in together. Then place the pan over medium heat.
The pan is on medium. Do I need to stir constantly while it heats?
Give it a few stirs so the sugar and salt dissolve evenly, then watch for it to come to a boil. You don't need aggressive stirring; just keep an eye on the surface and the heat.
It's starting to bubble around the edges but not fully boiling yet.
Let it reach a clear boil, then remove the saucepan from the heat right away. That off-heat move matters because the flour needs to be stirred in after the liquid mixture has boiled.
Okay, it boiled and I took it off the burner. What should the flour step look like?
Stir in the flour until the mixture comes together and forms a ball. It should pull away from the sides of the pan rather than staying loose or soupy.
It's thickening, but there are a couple of dry streaks left. Should I put it back on the heat?
Keep stirring off the heat for a bit longer first. The goal is one cohesive ball of dough; once the dry streaks disappear and it gathers together, you're ready to focus on the frying oil.
The dough has formed a ball. I'm using a deep skillet instead of a fryer—what temperature am I aiming for?
Heat the oil in the deep skillet to 375 degrees F, which is 190 degrees C. Use enough oil for frying safely, and check the temperature before adding any dough.
The oil is almost there. Any final checks before I start frying and serving?
Make sure the dough is holding together, the oil is at 375 degrees F or 190 degrees C, and your serving area is ready before frying. Keep the skillet steady and avoid crowding once you begin.
Can you walk me through Babis Bean Salad while I get everything set up?

Absolutely. Start by putting a saucepan on the stove and clearing space for the soaked beans and the chopped vegetables, since this salad begins with cooking the black-eyed peas and then cooling them.
The black-eyed peas soaked overnight. How much should I be using?
Use 1 1/2 cups dried black-eyed peas, already soaked overnight. Drain them if they're sitting in soaking water, then add them to the saucepan.
They're in the pan. How much water goes in with them?
Add enough water to cover the beans by 1 inch. Once they're covered, set the pan over heat and bring the beans to a slow boil.
While that heats, what vegetables and herbs should I have ready?
Keep 1/3 cup chopped celery with leaves, 1 1/2 cups shredded carrot, and 3/4 cup chopped fresh parsley nearby. Those are the other listed ingredients for Babis Bean Salad.
The water is starting to bubble gently. Is that the slow boil I want?
Yes, a gentle steady bubbling is right. Once you've reached that slow boil, reduce the heat to low so the beans can simmer without breaking apart.
How long should I let them simmer on low?
Simmer them until they're tender but not mushy, about 35 minutes. Check a bean near the end by tasting or pressing it; it should give easily but still hold its shape.
If some beans seem done before others, should I keep cooking?
Give the pot a gentle stir and check a few beans from different spots. If most are still firm, keep simmering briefly; if they're mostly tender and intact, stop before they turn mushy.
The beans are tender now. What should I do before mixing in the celery, carrot, and parsley?
Take the saucepan off the heat and set the beans aside to cool. Once they're no longer hot, you can combine them with the celery, shredded carrot, and fresh parsley for serving.
Can you walk me through making Easy Bake Oven Cookie Mix? I want to get the dry mix stored neatly.
Absolutely. Set out a medium bowl, measuring cups and spoons, a fork or pastry cutter for the shortening, and resealable bags or small containers for storing the mix.
I have the bowl and bags out. Which ingredients should I measure into the bowl?
Measure in 1 1/2 cups quick-cooking oats, 3/4 cup all-purpose flour, 1/4 teaspoon baking soda, and 3/4 cup packed brown sugar.
The oats, flour, baking soda, and brown sugar are measured. Should I mix them before adding anything else?
Yes. Stir those dry ingredients together in the medium bowl until the brown sugar is broken up and the oats, flour, and baking soda look evenly distributed.
The dry mix looks mostly even, but there are a couple of brown sugar clumps.
Press those clumps apart with the back of a spoon or your fingers, then stir again. You want an even mix before the shortening goes in.
Okay, the clumps are gone. How do I work in the shortening?
Add the shortening and cut it into the dry mixture with a fork or pastry cutter. Keep pressing and mixing until the whole bowl looks like coarse cornmeal.
It is starting to look sandy, but I can still see a few little shortening bits.
Keep cutting it in for another 2 minutes or so. The key check is that there should be no lumps of shortening left.
Now it looks like cornmeal all the way through. How should I portion it for storage?
Measure 1/2 cup of the mixture into each resealable bag or container. Level each portion so the bags are consistent.
The bags are filled. Anything I should do before putting them away?
Seal the bags or containers tightly, label them as Easy Bake Oven Cookie Mix, and add the date. Store them in a cool, dry spot until you are ready to use the mix.
Can you guide me through Crab Quiche while I get the counter set up?
Absolutely. Clear a spot for a 9 inch deep dish frozen pie crust, a mixing bowl, a whisk, and a baking sheet if you like using one for easier handling.
I have the frozen crust out. What should I measure before the oven goes on?
Pull out 4 eggs, 1 cup heavy cream, and 1/2 teaspoon salt. You'll also need pepper and hot sauce when you mix the custard.
The eggs, cream, and salt are on the counter. Should I do anything to the crust before filling it?
Yes. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F, which is 175 degrees C. Keep the crust frozen for the moment while the oven heats.
The oven is almost heated, and the crust is still in its tin. How long does it bake empty?
Bake the pie crust for about 10 minutes. You're looking for it to just start browning, not turn deeply golden.
It has a little color around the edge after 10 minutes. Do I leave it in longer?
If it's just starting to brown, take it out now. Set it on a heat-safe surface and let it cool before you add the egg mixture.
While the crust cools, should I mix the filling all at once?
Use a large bowl and whisk together the 4 eggs, 1 cup heavy cream, 1/2 teaspoon salt, pepper, and hot sauce until the mixture looks even.
How smooth should that egg and cream mixture be?
Whisk until the yolks and cream are fully blended and you don't see streaks of egg white. A few bubbles on top are fine.
The crust is cooler and the bowl is mixed. Anything to check before I pour?
Make sure the crust is no longer hot to the touch, the custard is evenly whisked, and the pie shell is sitting level so the filling won't spill.
Can you walk me through German Chocolate Brownie Cookies while I set up the counter?

Absolutely. Put a large mixing bowl in your work area and set out the brown sugar, shortening, water, and vanilla. You'll also want a second bowl ready for the flour, cocoa, salt, and baking soda later.
I've got the bowls out. Which measured ingredients should go near the large bowl?
Measure 1 1/2 cups packed brown sugar, 2/3 cup shortening, 1 tablespoon water, and 1 teaspoon vanilla extract. Those all start together in the large bowl.
The brown sugar is packed and the shortening is measured. Do I stir them by hand or cream them?

Add the brown sugar, shortening, water, and vanilla to the large bowl, then beat them together until the mixture looks creamy and fairly even. Scrape the bowl once so the shortening doesn't stay in streaks.
The mixture looks creamy now. I have the eggs nearby—when do they go in?
Beat the eggs into the creamed mixture now. Add them one at a time if that's easier to keep the batter smooth, and stop once they're fully incorporated.
The eggs are mixed in. What should I put in the other bowl?
In the second bowl, combine the flour, cocoa, salt, and baking soda. Whisk or stir them together so the cocoa and baking soda are evenly distributed before they meet the wet mixture.
The dry bowl is mixed. Should I dump it all in at once?
Add the dry mixture into the creamed mixture gradually if you want better control. Mix only until just blended, because overmixing can make the cookies less tender.
I can still see a few dry streaks along the edge of the bowl. Keep mixing?
Yes, but just briefly. Scrape around the sides and bottom, then fold or mix until those dry streaks disappear. Stop as soon as the batter looks unified.
Before I move on to baking or portioning, what should I check in the dough?

Check that the batter is evenly chocolate-colored, with no pockets of flour or cocoa, and that the texture is thick and blended rather than runny. Once it's just combined, you're ready to portion it according to your recipe card.
I'm making Aunt Mamies and want to get everything set up before I start mixing. What should I pull out first?

Set out the softened dairy ingredients: 1 (8 ounce) package cream cheese and 1/2 cup butter, softened. You'll also want a mixing bowl, beaters or a sturdy spoon, measuring cups, plastic wrap or a cover, and space in the fridge for chilling.
I've got the cream cheese and butter on the counter. What dry ingredients should I measure before the bowl gets messy?
Measure 2 cups all-purpose flour and 1 cup white sugar. Keep the flour near the mixing bowl, and keep the sugar by a small saucepan because it's used later with milk over medium heat.
The cream cheese is soft and the butter gives when I press it. Do I beat those together right away?

Yes. Beat the cream cheese with the margarine called for in the directions until the mixture looks smooth and well blended. Since your ingredient list has softened butter, use that here unless your recipe card specifically says otherwise.
It's mostly smooth, but I still see a few pale streaks. Should I add flour yet?
Give it a little more mixing until the streaks are mostly gone and the texture is even. Once it looks creamy and combined, add the flour.
All right, I'm adding the flour. Do I dump in both cups at once or work it in gradually?
You can add the 2 cups all-purpose flour in portions if that's easier to control. Mix well after each addition so the dough comes together without dry pockets.
The dough is thick now and pulling away from the side of the bowl. What should it feel like before chilling?
It should be cohesive enough to gather into a ball. Shape it into a ball, cover it, and chill it for 2 hours so it firms up.
The dough is covered and in the fridge. While it chills, should I do anything with the saucepan step?

You can stage the saucepan and have the 1 cup white sugar ready, but wait to cook it with the milk until you're ready for that step. The recipe doesn't give a milk amount, so use the amount from your card if it's written elsewhere.
The 2 hours are up. For the sugar and milk, what am I watching for on the stove?
Put the sugar and milk in a saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally. Keep cooking until the milk boils and the sugar is dissolved; it should look smooth rather than grainy before you serve.
Can you walk me through Flax and Sunflower Seed Bread in the bread machine? I've got the pan out and want to keep it simple.
Absolutely. Set the bread-machine pan on the counter first, and gather 1 1/3 cups water, 2 tablespoons softened butter, 3 tablespoons honey, 1 1/2 cups bread flour, and the sunflower seeds for later.
I have the water measured and the butter is soft. Does everything go straight into the pan?
Add the ingredients to the bread-machine pan in the order your machine's manufacturer recommends. Hold back the sunflower seeds for now; they go in during the knead cycle when the machine alerts you.
My machine usually wants liquids first, so I'm putting in the 1 1/3 cups water. Should honey go in with that?
Yes, if your machine calls for liquids first, add the 3 tablespoons honey after the water, then add the 2 tablespoons softened butter.
The wet ingredients are in the pan. I'm about to add the flour—anything special with the 1 1/2 cups bread flour?
Spoon and level the 1 1/2 cups bread flour if you haven't measured it yet, then add it evenly over the wet ingredients in the pan. Try not to splash the liquid up the sides.
Flour is in. The sunflower seeds are still sitting in a small bowl beside the machine.
Great. Put the pan into the bread machine, close the lid, select the basic white cycle, and press start.
It started mixing. The dough is coming together, but the seeds are not in yet.
That's right—wait for the machine's alert during the knead cycle. When it sounds, open the lid briefly and add the sunflower seeds, then close it again so the cycle can continue.
The alert just beeped, and I added the sunflower seeds. The dough looks a little uneven right now.
That can happen right after the seed addition. Let the knead cycle work them in; the machine should distribute the sunflower seeds as it continues.
What should I do near the end of the cycle so I don't mess up the loaf?

Let the basic white cycle finish completely before removing the pan. Once it's done, take the bread out carefully, let it cool enough to slice cleanly, and check that the texture looks set before serving.
I'm making Grandmas Wheat Germ Cookies. Can you help me get the dry ingredients organized before I start mixing?
Yes. Pull out a large mixing bowl and measure the dry base into it: 1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 1/2 cups toasted wheat germ, 1 cup quick-cooking oats, and 1 cup packed brown sugar.
Those are in the bowl. The recipe says to combine the first six ingredients, but I want to make sure I'm not missing the last two.

Add 2 teaspoons baking powder and 1 teaspoon salt to that same bowl, then stir the dry ingredients together so the baking powder and salt are evenly spread through the flour, wheat germ, oats, and brown sugar.
The dry mixture looks even. What should I use for the wet bowl?
In a separate bowl, combine the applesauce, oil, and eggs. Whisk them until the eggs are fully broken up and the mixture looks smooth enough to pour.
The wet mixture is ready. Should I dump it all into the flour mixture or add it slowly?
Pour the applesauce, oil, and egg mixture into the flour mixture and mix well. Scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl so no dry pockets stay hidden, but stop once everything is evenly moistened.
It's thick now, more like cookie dough. I still have chocolate chips and walnuts on the counter.
Stir in the chocolate chips and walnuts gently. Fold them through the dough until they're distributed, rather than beating the dough hard.
I'm getting the baking sheets ready. The dough is sticky on the spoon.
Coat the baking sheets with nonstick cooking spray, then drop the dough by rounded teaspoonfuls onto the sheets, leaving them 2 in apart so the cookies have room.
The mounds are spaced out. Do they need shaping before they go in?
Yes, flatten each mound slightly with the bottom of a glass coated with nonstick cooking spray. Recoat the glass if it starts sticking to the dough.
They're flattened and ready. What should I watch for while they bake and when they come off the sheet?

Watch for the cookies to look set around the edges and no longer wet on top. Let them firm up briefly on the baking sheet, then move them carefully so they keep their shape and the texture stays tender.
I'm making Broccoli Coleslaw and want to keep it simple. Can you talk me through what to set out before I start mixing?

Set out 1 cup olive oil, 1/3 cup distilled white vinegar, 1/2 cup white sugar, and 1 (3 ounce) package chicken flavored ramen noodles. Keep the ramen seasoning packet because it goes into the dressing, and crush the noodles separately for later.
I've got the oil, vinegar, sugar, and ramen packet on the counter. What bowl should I use for the dressing?

Use a small bowl for the dressing. Whisk together the olive oil, distilled white vinegar, white sugar, and the reserved seasoning packet from the ramen until the sugar starts dissolving and the mixture looks even.
The dressing is mixed but still a little grainy from the sugar. Is that okay before chilling?
That's fine as long as it's well mixed. Cover it and refrigerate it for at least 1 hour before serving, or overnight if you're making it ahead.
While the dressing chills, I'm prepping the vegetables. What goes in the big bowl?
In a large bowl, combine the broccoli, carrots, green onions, and sunflower seeds. Keep the pieces bite-size so the dressing can coat everything evenly.
I have the broccoli diced and the carrots and green onions added. Should the sunflower seeds go in now or at the end?
Add the sunflower seeds now with the vegetables. They'll mix through the slaw better before the dressing goes on.
The ramen noodles are still in the package. How fine should I crush them?
Crush the ramen noodles into small, crunchy pieces rather than powder. Stir them into the broccoli mixture so they're spread throughout the bowl.
The salad bowl is ready and the dressing has been chilling for about an hour. When do I combine them?
Pour the dressing over the salad about 10 minutes before serving. Toss well so the broccoli, carrots, green onions, sunflower seeds, and crushed ramen all get coated.
What should I check right before I put it on the table?
Check that the dressing is evenly distributed, the ramen still has some crunch, and the slaw tastes balanced between sweet and tangy. Give it one more toss before serving.
I'm making Dads Flat Bread and I've got a large mixing bowl out. Can you walk me through what to measure before I start?

Set out 1 (.25 ounce) package active dry yeast, 2 cups warm water at 110° to 115°, 1/3 cup sugar, and 2 tablespoons vegetable oil. You'll also want salt, rye or whole wheat flour, and all-purpose flour nearby for the dough.
The warm water is ready. Do I use all 2 cups with the yeast?
Use only 1/2 cup of the warm water to dissolve the yeast in the large mixing bowl. Keep the remaining warm water aside for the next mix-in.
The yeast is in the 1/2 cup water and looks dissolved. What goes into the bowl with it?
Add the 1/3 cup sugar, 2 tablespoons vegetable oil, salt, rye or whole wheat flour, 3 cups all-purpose flour, and the remaining warm water. Beat everything until the mixture looks smooth.
I see salt and whole wheat flour in the recipe notes, but I want to make sure I'm not overdoing either one.
Use 1 tablespoon salt and 1/2 cup rye or whole wheat flour. Those go in with the sugar, oil, 3 cups all-purpose flour, and the rest of the warm water before you beat the mixture smooth.
The dough mixture is smooth but still loose. Should I dump in the rest of the flour at once?
Add the remaining all-purpose flour gradually, just enough to form a soft dough. Stop when it holds together and feels workable rather than stiff or dry.
It's coming together now. My counter is floured—how should the kneading feel?
Turn the dough onto the floured surface and knead until it becomes smooth and elastic, about 6-8 minutes. If it sticks badly, dust lightly with flour, but avoid working in more than you need.
I'm about 4 minutes into kneading, and it's less sticky but still a little tacky.
That sounds on track. Keep kneading through the 6-8 minute window; the surface should smooth out, and the dough should spring back a bit when pressed.
Once it feels smooth, what should I do before I think about serving or shaping it further?
Place the dough in a greased bowl, turning it once so the top is greased too. Cover it and let it rise in a warm place until doubled, about 1 hour, then check the texture before moving on.
I'm making Cawl Traditional Welsh Broth with beef shank, onions, and carrots. Can you help me set up before I turn on the stove?

Absolutely. Put a large pot on the stove and set out 2 quarts water, 12 ounces beef shank, 2 large chopped onions, and 2 large sliced carrots. Keep a cutting board and knife nearby for later, when the cooked meat needs trimming.
The pot is out. Should the onions and carrots go in right away with the water?
Start by bringing the 2 quarts water to a boil in the large pot. Hold the onions and carrots aside for now, since the recipe's next cooking move is focused on simmering the beef shank.
The water is close to boiling, and the beef shank is still in one piece. Is that okay?
Yes, leave the beef shank whole at this point. Once the water is boiling, lower it in carefully, then adjust the heat so it simmers steadily rather than rolling hard.
It's simmering now. How long should I keep it there?
Let the beef shank simmer for 1 1/2 hours. Keep the pot at a gentle simmer, with small bubbles rising, and check occasionally that the meat stays covered by the broth.
After about an hour, the broth is bubbling more strongly than before. Should I turn it down?
Yes, turn the heat down enough to return it to a calm simmer. You want steady cooking for the full 1 1/2 hours, not a hard boil that can make the broth cloudy and jostle the meat too much.
The 1 1/2 hours are done. The meat looks cooked and the broth is hot. What happens next?
Take the pot off the heat and let it cool, then refrigerate it overnight. Don't trim the meat yet; the recipe has you cool the broth first, then lift the meat out the next day.
It's the next day, and the broth is chilled. There's meat and some firm bits around it. What should I do on the board?
Lift the beef shank out of the cooled broth and put it on the cutting board. Trim off the gristle, then cut the meat into medium-sized pieces and set those pieces aside.
The meat is cut up. I still have the chopped onions and sliced carrots ready—how should I keep everything organized?

Keep the trimmed meat separate from the 2 large chopped onions and 2 large sliced carrots until you continue with the rest of your recipe card. At this point, you've completed the listed prep: boiled the water, simmered the 12 ounces beef shank, cooled it overnight, trimmed off gristle, and cut the meat into medium-sized pieces.
Can you guide me through Bruschetta II 2? I've got a baking sheet and want to keep it simple.

Absolutely. Gather 10 slices Italian bread, 2 1/2 teaspoons olive oil, 4 vine-ripened tomatoes, and 1 teaspoon chopped fresh basil. You'll also want a medium baking sheet, a pastry brush or spoon, a knife, and a cutting board.
The ingredients are on the counter. Should I deal with the bread or tomatoes first?
Start by preheating the broiler so it's ready when the bread is arranged. While it heats, keep the tomatoes nearby for dicing.
Broiler is heating. How should the bread go on the pan?
Lay the 10 Italian bread slices on the medium baking sheet in a single layer, not stacked, so each slice can catch the broiler evenly.
They fit in one layer. Do I use all the oil on top?
Brush the bread slices with the 2 1/2 teaspoons olive oil. Try to spread it lightly and evenly across the slices rather than soaking any one piece.
The bread is brushed. What size should I cut the tomatoes?
Dice the 4 vine-ripened tomatoes into small pieces that will sit easily on the bread. Aim for spoonable pieces rather than large chunks.
Tomatoes are diced. Where does the basil come in?
Add the 1 teaspoon chopped fresh basil to the diced tomatoes, then toss gently so the basil is distributed without crushing the tomatoes.
The tomato and basil mixture looks juicy. Should I put it on the bread before broiling?

For this recipe's listed flow, the key prep is the broiler, the single layer of bread, the olive oil on the slices, and the diced tomatoes. If you're topping the bread now, spoon the tomato mixture on carefully so the slices don't get overloaded.
I'm ready to serve these. What final check should I make?

Check that the bread slices are still in a neat single layer, the oil is evenly brushed, and the diced tomato-basil topping is balanced across the pieces. Serve right away so the bread stays pleasant instead of turning soggy.
Can you walk me through Eggnog II while I set up and cook it? I want to avoid scrambling the eggs.
Absolutely. Use a large saucepan, a spoon for constant stirring, and either a sink or bowl ready for ice water later so you can cool the custard quickly.
I have the saucepan out. What ingredients should I measure before the heat goes on?
Measure 6 beaten eggs, 2 1/4 cups milk, and 1/3 cup white sugar. Those three go together in the large saucepan before cooking.
Should the vanilla go in the pan with the eggs, milk, and sugar?
Keep the 1 teaspoon vanilla extract measured nearby, but don't add it to the saucepan yet. Start by combining only the beaten eggs, milk, and white sugar.
The eggs, milk, and sugar are in the saucepan. How hot should I set the burner?
Set it to medium heat. Stir steadily and keep the spoon moving across the bottom and corners of the pan so the egg mixture thickens evenly.
What am I looking for so I know it has cooked enough?
Cook and stir until the mixture coats a metal spoon. It should cling lightly to the spoon instead of running off immediately.
It's starting to thicken, and I'm worried about taking it too far.
Lower your pace only by removing the pan from the heat as soon as it coats the metal spoon. Don't keep it on the burner after that point.
The pan is off the stove. What do I do with the ice water setup?
Place the pan in a sink or bowl of ice water and stir the eggnog for 1 to 2 minutes. That quick cooling helps protect the texture.
It has cooled for about 2 minutes. Where does the vanilla fit in before serving?
Stir in the 1 teaspoon vanilla extract now, then give the eggnog a final smooth stir before serving.
I'm making Cinnamon Rolls I in the bread machine. I've got counter space cleared, but I want to stage things sensibly before I start.

Set the bread machine pan nearby and start with the dough ingredients you listed: 1 cup warm water at 110 degrees F, 1 egg, 3 cups bread flour, and 1/4 cup white sugar. Keep measuring cups and a spoon handy so you can load the pan in the manufacturer's recommended order.
The water is at 110 degrees F and the egg is out. Should the wet ingredients go in before the flour?

Yes, follow your bread machine's order. If it calls for liquids first, add the warm water and egg, then the bread flour and white sugar. The recipe also has powdered milk, salt, 5 tablespoons butter, and yeast going into the machine with those dough ingredients.
I've added the water, egg, flour, sugar, powdered milk, salt, butter, and yeast to the pan. Anything to check before I close it?
Make sure the pan is seated firmly, the yeast is where your machine expects it, and no dry flour is caught on the rim. Then close the lid and choose the DOUGH setting.
The DOUGH setting is on. While it runs, I want to get the topping started without getting ahead of myself.

Good timing. While the dough cycle is running, place a small saucepan on the stove and melt 1/3 cup butter over gentle heat. Stir as it melts so it doesn't brown unless your recipe specifically calls for that.
The 1/3 cup butter is melted. The recipe says brown sugar and ice cream next—how should I handle that?
Add 1/2 cup brown sugar and the ice cream to the melted butter. Stir the mixture as it heats so the sugar dissolves and the ice cream blends in smoothly.
It's blended and starting to bubble around the edges. Do I boil it hard?
Bring it to a boil, then cook it for 2 minutes. Keep stirring and use steady heat so the sauce cooks evenly without scorching on the bottom of the saucepan.
The sauce has boiled for 2 minutes. It looks glossy but a little hot and thin right now.
That's expected right off the heat. Let it stand briefly so the bubbling settles, then check that the texture is smooth and pourable before you use it with the rolls.
The dough cycle is still going. Is there anything useful to clean or prepare before shaping and serving later?

Wipe the counter, set out a rolling surface, and keep the sauce nearby once it has settled. When the dough is ready, you'll be in good shape to move from the bread machine to shaping, baking, and serving without scrambling.
Can you walk me through Broiled Egg Salad Sandwiches? I've got the eggs cooked already and want to stay organized.
Absolutely. Clear a little counter space for 2 bowls, a spoon, and an ungreased baking sheet. Have the muffin halves nearby for topping later.
What ingredients should I pull out before I start mixing anything?
Set out 3 hard-cooked eggs, chopped, plus 1/4 cup crushed saltine crackers. Those will go into the main bowl together.
Eggs and crackers are ready. What else goes in that same bowl?
Add 1/4 cup chopped celery and 1 tablespoon diced pimientos to that bowl. Give the ingredients a light toss so the crackers, celery, and pimientos are spread through the chopped eggs.
The egg mixture looks evenly combined. Do I add mayonnaise straight into it?
Use a second bowl first. Combine the mayonnaise, milk, salt, garlic salt, and pepper there, then mix well so the dressing is smooth before it touches the eggs.
I've mixed the dressing. It's creamy but still loose enough to stir.
That sounds right. Pour or spoon the dressing into the egg mixture and stir gently until everything is coated without mashing the eggs too much.
The filling is together. Should it be chunky or more like a spread?
It should stay a little chunky from the chopped eggs and celery, with the dressing holding it together. If the crackers are visible in spots, that is fine as long as the mixture is evenly moistened.
I've got the muffin halves on the counter. How much filling goes on each one?
Spoon about 1/3 cup of the egg salad mixture onto each muffin half. Try to keep the filling centered so it sits neatly on the bread.
They're topped. What do I do with the baking sheet?
Place the topped muffin halves on an ungreased baking sheet. Before serving or broiling, check that each portion is steady, the filling is evenly spread, and the sheet is ready to move safely.
Can you guide me through Broccoli Chicken Roli while I set up the counter?

Absolutely. Put out a large mixing bowl, a cookie sheet, aluminum foil, and the ingredients you'll be combining: 2 cups chopped cooked chicken, 2 cups fresh chopped broccoli, 1/2 cup chopped onion, and 1/2 cup chopped green bell pepper.
I've got the bowl and vegetables out. Does the chicken go in cold, or should I warm it first?

Use the chicken already cooked and chopped; it can go straight into the bowl as long as it's safe and ready to eat. Add it with the chopped broccoli, onion, and green bell pepper so the main filling starts evenly mixed.
The vegetables are chopped. What else belongs in that filling before I stir?

Add the cheese, mayonnaise, mustard, salt, pepper, and garlic to the same bowl. If you're using the amount from your notes, include 1 1/2 cups shredded Cheddar cheese, then keep the mayonnaise and mustard distributed through the chicken and vegetables as you mix.
The bowl is getting full. Should I fold it gently or really mash it together?

Fold and stir until everything is coated and combined, but don't mash the broccoli. You want the chicken, broccoli, onion, bell pepper, cheese, mayonnaise, mustard, salt, pepper, and garlic mixed into one even filling.
The mixture looks fairly even now. Should the oven be on yet?
Yes, preheat the oven to 400 degrees F, which is 200 degrees C. While it heats, line the cookie sheet with aluminum foil.
Foil is on the pan. The recipe note mentions a glass—where does that fit?

Place a glass upside down in the center of the foil-covered cookie sheet. That gives you a center guide before arranging the roli mixture or dough around it, depending on how your recipe card continues.
If the filling seems wetter than expected, should I add something to dry it out?

Don't add a new ingredient unless your recipe card calls for it. Stir once more to redistribute the mayonnaise and cheese, then check that the mixture holds together enough to place around the center glass.
Before I put it in the oven, what should I double-check on the pan?

Make sure the foil is covering the cookie sheet, the upside-down glass is centered, the filling is evenly mixed, and the oven has reached 400 degrees F / 200 degrees C. Also confirm the chicken was already cooked before you started assembling.
Can you walk me through Enchilada Style Burritos while I get the baking dish and saucepan ready?
Absolutely. Grease a 13-in baking dish first, then place the 6 frozen prepared bean and cheese burritos in it and set the dish aside while you make the sauce base.
The burritos are in the greased dish. What should I measure before I turn on the burner?
Measure 2 tablespoons butter or margarine, 3 tablespoons all-purpose flour, and 1 3/4 cups water. Keep the flour close to the saucepan because it goes in right after the butter melts.
I also found a 1 (8 ounce) can of tomato sauce near my ingredients. Should that be part of this?

Use the ingredient list in front of you as the guide: the version you gave me calls for the burritos, butter or margarine, flour, and water. If the tomato sauce is from another version, leave it aside unless your recipe card specifically includes it.
Got it. The saucepan is on the stove with the butter in it. How hot should I go?
Use moderate heat so the butter melts without browning fast. Once it is fully melted and looks even across the bottom of the pan, you are ready for the flour.
The butter is melted. I am worried the flour will clump.
Sprinkle in the 3 tablespoons flour while stirring steadily. Keep stirring until the mixture looks smooth before you add any water.
It looks smooth now. Do I pour in all the water at once?
Add the 1 3/4 cups water gradually, stirring as you pour. That slow addition helps the sauce base stay smooth instead of turning lumpy.
The water is in and the mixture is loosening. What am I waiting for?
Bring it to a boil, then cook and stir for 2 minutes or until it thickens. Keep the spoon moving so the bottom of the saucepan does not catch.
It has thickened after about 2 minutes. What should I check before serving the burritos?

Make sure the burritos are still arranged neatly in the greased baking dish and the thickened sauce base is smooth. Spoon it over the burritos as your recipe directs, then serve once everything is hot and evenly coated.
Can you talk me through Easy Pavlova while I set up and bake it?
Absolutely. Start by preheating the oven to 300 degrees F, or 150 degrees C, so it is ready when the meringue is shaped.
The oven is heating. What should I put on the counter before I crack the eggs?

Set out 4 egg whites, 1 1/4 cups white sugar, 1 teaspoon vanilla extract, and 1 teaspoon lemon juice. You will also want a large clean bowl, beaters, a baking sheet, parchment paper, and a pencil for marking the guide circle.
I also have 2 teaspoons cornstarch sitting here from another pavlova note. Should I use it in this one?

Use the ingredient list for this Easy Pavlova: egg whites, white sugar, vanilla extract, and lemon juice. Since 2 teaspoons cornstarch is not in the recipe you are following, leave it out unless your own recipe card specifically includes it.
Got it. I have the baking sheet and parchment ready. How do I mark it without making a mess?

Line the baking sheet with parchment paper, then draw a 9 inch circle on the parchment as your shaping guide. If you use pencil, flip the parchment over so the meringue will not touch the pencil marks.
The circle is marked and flipped. Before I start whipping, anything important about the bowl or egg whites?
Make sure the bowl and beaters are clean and dry, and that no yolk got into the 4 egg whites. Then beat the egg whites in the large bowl until they are stiff but not dry.
What does stiff but not dry look like? I do not want to overbeat them.
When you lift the beaters, the peaks should stand up firmly and look glossy. Stop before the whites turn grainy, clumpy, or dull.
They are glossy and holding peaks. When does the sugar go in?
Add the 1 1/4 cups white sugar gradually, about 1 tablespoon at a time, beating well after each addition so the meringue stays smooth and stable.
The sugar is mostly mixed in. Where do the vanilla and lemon juice fit before I spread it?

Beat in 1 teaspoon vanilla extract and 1 teaspoon lemon juice, then spoon the meringue onto the 9 inch circle. Shape it neatly within the guide, check that the texture is still glossy, and bake according to the recipe once the oven is at 300 degrees F.
Can you guide me through Artichoke and Sun dried Tomato Chicken while I cook? I've got the skillet out.

Absolutely. Put the 4 skinless, boneless chicken breast halves near your board, along with salt, pepper, 2 teaspoons olive oil, the 1 (14.5 ounce) can diced tomatoes with green peppers and onions, and 1/4 cup sun-dried tomato pesto if it's on your recipe card.
The chicken is still in the package. Should I season before the pan heats?
Yes. Pat the chicken dry if needed, then season both sides with salt and pepper. That way it's ready to go as soon as the oil is hot.
Seasoned. I'm opening the tomatoes now so I'm not scrambling later.
Good idea. Open the 14.5 ounce can and keep it close to the stove. If you're using the 1/4 cup sun-dried tomato pesto, measure that now too, but keep it separate from the raw chicken area.
Pan is on the burner. How hot should I take it?
Set the large skillet over medium-high heat and add the 2 teaspoons olive oil. Give the oil a short moment to shimmer before the chicken goes in.
The oil looks shiny and moves easily when I tilt the pan.
That's the cue. Lay the chicken breasts into the skillet in a single layer. Let them brown on the first side without moving them around too much.
They're sizzling pretty hard. Should I flip them more than once?
Turn them once to brown the other side. If the sizzling sounds harsh or the fond is getting too dark, lower the heat a little, but keep the goal to brown both sides.
Both sides have color now, but I know they aren't fully finished.
That's fine for this stage. Remove the chicken from the pan and set it aside on a clean plate so you can use the browned bits left in the skillet.
The pan has browned bits and a little oil left. Do the tomatoes go in now?

Yes. Pour the diced tomatoes with green peppers and onions into the pan and stir constantly for 1 minute, scraping up the browned bits from the bottom. Stir in the sun-dried tomato pesto if your card includes it, then check the sauce texture and taste before serving with the chicken.

source_seed.recipe_title: Artichoke and Sun dried Tomato Chicken

messages.content: I'm making Cinnamon Crackle Cookies today. Can you guide me while I get the ingredients and pans ready?
Absolutely. Set out a mixing bowl, measuring cups, ungreased baking sheets, and a small bowl or plate for rolling the dough balls in sugar later.
I've got the bowl and baking sheets out. Which fats and sugars should go in the bowl?
Add 1/2 cup softened butter, 1/2 cup shortening, 1 cup sugar, and 1/2 cup packed brown sugar to the mixing bowl. Cream them together until the mixture looks lighter and well blended.
The butter and shortening are soft, but the brown sugar is clumpy. Should I break it up before measuring?
Yes, break up any firm clumps, then pack it into the measuring cup so you still have 1/2 cup packed brown sugar. That helps it mix evenly with the butter, shortening, and sugar.
The creamed mixture looks smooth now. What do I add next?
Add the egg and the extracts, then mix well. Scrape the sides of the bowl so everything gets incorporated before the dry ingredients go in.
I'm ready for the dry ingredients, but the recipe says to combine the next eight ingredients. How should I handle that?
Whisk those eight dry ingredients together in a separate bowl first. Once they're evenly combined, add them gradually to the creamed mixture rather than dumping them in all at once.
The dough is thickening as I add the dry mixture. Is that expected?
Yes, cookie dough should get thicker at this stage. Keep mixing just until the dry ingredients disappear into the creamed mixture; stop before it looks overworked.
The dough is mixed. How should I portion it for the baking sheets?
Shape the dough into 1-in balls, then roll each ball in sugar. Place them on ungreased baking sheets with room between them so they can spread a bit.
The trays are loaded. What oven setting and timing should I use, and how do I know they're done?

Bake them at 350 degrees F, which is 177 degrees C, for 10-15 minutes, or until they're lightly browned. Let them settle briefly on the baking sheets before moving them so the crackled tops stay intact.
I'm making Diegos Special Beef Stew. Can you walk me through the setup before I turn on the stove?

Absolutely. Pull out 1 pound cubed beef stew meat, 1 tablespoon all-purpose flour, 2 tablespoons olive oil, and 2 teaspoons butter. You'll also want a resealable plastic bag, a skillet, tongs or a spatula, and your slow cooker ready nearby.
I've got the beef and flour out. Does the butter go in now too?
Not for the coating step. Keep the 2 teaspoons butter measured and set aside. Right now, put the cubed beef and 1 tablespoon all-purpose flour into the resealable plastic bag.
The beef and flour are in the bag. How much should I shake it?
Seal the bag well, then shake and turn it until the beef pieces are evenly coated with flour. You're looking for a light, even dusting rather than clumps of dry flour.
Some flour is sticking in the corners of the bag. Is that a problem?
That's fine as long as the beef itself is coated. If a few dry bits stay in the corners, just tap the bag and give it another quick shake before opening it.
Okay, the beef looks coated. What should I do at the skillet?
Set the skillet over medium heat and add the 2 tablespoons olive oil. Let the oil warm briefly so the beef can brown instead of just sit in the pan.
Should I add all the beef at once, or is crowding going to mess up the browning?
Add the coated beef in a single layer if your skillet has room. If it looks crowded, brown it in batches so the pieces can make contact with the hot surface.
The first side is browning. How dark should I let it get?
Brown the beef on all sides over medium heat. Aim for a good browned surface, but move the pieces before the flour coating gets too dark or starts to scorch.
The beef is browned. Where does it go from here?

Transfer the browned beef to the slow cooker. Scrape up any browned bits that come along easily, keep the 2 teaspoons butter with your staged ingredients, and make sure the slow cooker is ready for the next part of the stew.
I'm getting ready to make BBQ Chuck Roast. Can you help me set up the marinade without overcomplicating it?

Absolutely. Pull out the 1 (5 pound) chuck roast, a large bowl, 1 cup barbeque sauce, 1 cup teriyaki sauce, and 1 (12 fluid ounce) can or bottle of beer. Those are the main items to get the marinade started.
I have those on the counter. The recipe also mentions aromatics—what should I measure before I start mixing?
Measure 3 teaspoons minced garlic and 3 teaspoons thinly sliced fresh ginger root. Also have onion, black pepper, and salt ready, since those get mixed into the bowl with the sauces and beer.
Should I put the roast in right after the marinade is mixed?

Yes. Mix the barbeque sauce, teriyaki sauce, beer, garlic, ginger, onion, black pepper, and salt in the large bowl, then place the chuck roast into that marinade. Cover it and refrigerate it for six hours, turning it often so the roast gets coated evenly.
It's been marinating for a while, and I've turned it a few times. What should I set up before it comes out of the fridge?
Get the outdoor grill ready for indirect heat. You'll also want a saucepan nearby, because when the roast comes out of the marinade, the marinade gets poured into the saucepan rather than discarded.
The grill is heating for indirect cooking. Do I drain the roast completely?
Lift the roast out of the marinade and let the excess drip back into the bowl for a moment. Then move the roast toward the grill area, and pour the remaining marinade into the saucepan.
I'm concerned about using the marinade after raw beef was in it. What makes it safe here?
The recipe has you bring that marinade to a boil and cook it for 5 minutes. Keep it at a proper boil for the full time before using it as a basting sauce.
While that sauce boils, what should I watch so it doesn't get too thick or scorched?
Use moderate heat once it reaches a boil, stir as needed, and keep an eye on the bottom of the saucepan. You want it cooked for the 5 minutes, not reduced into a sticky paste before you baste.
The sauce has boiled for 5 minutes, and the roast is ready for the grill. Any last prep check before I start cooking it?

Set the boiled marinade aside as your basting sauce, keep a clean brush or spoon for applying it, and make sure the roast is positioned for indirect heat rather than directly over the hottest part of the grill.
I'm making Bacon Wrapped Hamburgers tonight. Can you guide me from setup through grilling?
Absolutely. Start by getting the grill ready for high heat so it can preheat while you mix the patties.
While the grill heats, what ingredients should I put near the mixing bowl?

Set out 1/2 cup shredded Cheddar cheese, 1 tablespoon grated Parmesan cheese, 1 small chopped onion, and 1 egg. You'll also need ketchup, Worcestershire sauce, salt, pepper, the ground beef, bacon slices, and toothpicks.
Do the cheese, onion, and egg go straight in with the beef?
Mix the flavor base first: in a large bowl, stir together the Cheddar, Parmesan, chopped onion, egg, ketchup, Worcestershire sauce, salt, and pepper until they're fairly even.
I have that mixture in the bowl. It looks loose but combined.
That's right. Crumble in the ground beef next, then mix it by hand just until the seasoning mixture is worked through. Try not to overwork it, or the burgers can get dense.
The beef mixture is combined. How should I portion it?
Shape it into 6 patties. Keep them similar in thickness so they cook evenly on the grill.
I've got the patties shaped, and the bacon is ready beside them.
Wrap 1 slice of bacon around each patty, then secure the bacon with toothpicks so it stays in place during grilling.
The grill is hot and the bacon is pinned. How long do these cook?
Place the patties on the preheated grill and cook them for 5 minutes per side, or until they're well done.
Before I serve them, what should I check?
Make sure the burgers are well done, the bacon is cooked around the outside, and the toothpicks are removed before serving.
I'm making Dads Kickin Jamaican Wings Mon and want to get the marinade started before the wings go in. What should I pull out first?

Set up the blender and measure 3 tablespoons Jamaican jerk seasoning blend with 3 tablespoons vegetable oil. Have 3 diced garlic cloves and a peeled, diced 1 inch piece of fresh ginger ready beside it.
I've got the blender jar out. The garlic and ginger are chopped; what else goes into that blend?
Add the chopped green onions and 12 slices of pickled jalapeno peppers to the blender with the jerk seasoning, oil, garlic, and ginger. Blend until the mixture looks thick and smooth.
The marinade is thick now and smells strong. Do I pour it over the wings or coat them one by one?
Dunk the wings directly in the mixture so they're well coated, then arrange them in a single layer on baking sheets. Try not to stack them, or the marinade won't sit evenly.
The wings are spread out on the baking sheets. Should I cover them before chilling?
Yes, cover the baking sheets with aluminum foil and refrigerate the wings for 8 hours, or overnight, so the jerk mixture has time to soak in.
They've marinated overnight. I'm taking the trays out now—what oven setting do I need?
Preheat the oven to 300 degrees F, which is 150 degrees C. Keep the foil on while the oven comes up to temperature unless your recipe notes say otherwise.
The oven is at temperature. Should the wings go in on the same trays they marinated on?
Use the arranged baking sheets if they're oven-safe and the wings are still in a single layer. Slide them into the preheated oven and bake the wings for 2 hours.
About halfway through, the kitchen smells spicy and the edges are darkening a little. Should I change the heat?
Stay with 300 degrees F unless something is burning. You can rotate the baking sheets for even cooking, but keep the temperature steady so the wings cook through during the full bake.
The 2 hours are up. What should I check before I put them on a platter?
Look for wings that are cooked through, coated with the thick jerk mixture, and no longer wet-looking on the surface. Let them sit briefly, tidy the tray edges, then serve while they're hot.
Can you walk me through Gerry's Chicken Enchiladas while I prep the chicken, skillet, and baking dish?
Absolutely. Put the 4 boneless, skinless chicken breast halves on your board, grab a medium bowl for marinating, and keep a large skillet ready for the stovetop.
The chicken is on the board. How should I cut it before it goes in the bowl?
Cut the chicken breasts into 1 inch strips. Try to keep the pieces fairly even so they marinate and brown at the same pace.
The strips are cut. I have the bowl out, but I'm not sure about the timing for the marinade.
Place the chicken strips in the medium bowl with your desired marinade, cover it, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes.
While that chills, what vegetables and canned items should I line up?

Set out 1 onion, chopped, plus 1 (10 ounce) can diced tomatoes with green chile peppers. If your recipe card includes it, also keep the 1 (14.5 ounce) can stewed tomatoes nearby so you can confirm it before cooking.
The chicken has marinated for 30 minutes, and the onion is chopped. Should I start the oven or the skillet first?
Start by preheating the oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), then move to the skillet while the oven comes up to temperature.
The oven is heating. I've got the large skillet on the stove—what goes in?
Add 1 tablespoon vegetable oil to the large skillet and heat it over medium heat. Give the oil a moment to shimmer before adding the food.
The oil is shimmering. Do I add the marinated chicken and onion together?
Yes, add the chicken strips and chopped onion to the skillet. Saute them over medium heat until the chicken is evenly brown and the onion has softened.
The chicken is browning, but I don't want the texture to get dry before the enchiladas are assembled.
Keep the heat at medium and watch for even browning rather than pushing it hotter. Before serving later, check the taste, texture, and how everything is placed on the dish.
Can you walk me through Grandmas Carrot Cake while I get the counter set up?
Absolutely. Clear a little space for measuring, keep a 9x13 inch pan nearby, and have the oven ready to preheat once your ingredients are out.
I've got the pan and mixing bowl out. Which dry ingredients should I measure first?
Measure 2 cups all-purpose flour and 2 teaspoons baking soda into your prep area. Keep them dry and separate until you're ready to sift.
Those are measured. I still have my spice jar and sugar canister on the counter.
Great—add 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon to your measured dry ingredients, and set out 2 cups white sugar so everything listed is accounted for before you start heating the oven.
All four ingredients are out. Should I turn on the oven now or grease the pan first?
Go ahead and preheat the oven to 350 degrees F, which is 175 degrees C. While it heats, you can handle the pan.
The oven is preheating. What's the best way to prep the pan so I don't miss the corners?
Grease the 9x13 inch pan evenly, paying attention to the corners and sides so the cake batter won't cling later.
Pan is greased. I'm ready to combine the dry stuff—what exactly goes through the sifter?
Sift together the flour, baking soda, and cinnamon. The goal is an even dry mix with no clumps of baking soda or cinnamon.
The sifted mixture is in the bowl. Does the sugar go in with that right away?

The recipe steps you're following only say to sift the flour, baking soda, and cinnamon, then set that mixture aside. Keep the 2 cups white sugar measured and ready, but don't add it to this sifted bowl unless your full recipe card tells you to.
Okay, the dry bowl is off to the side and the oven is still coming up to temperature. Anything to check before I continue?

Make sure the greased 9x13 inch pan is ready, the sifted flour mixture is set aside, and your measured sugar is still within reach. Once the oven reaches 350 degrees F, you'll be lined up for the next part of the recipe.
